definition: Cyborg data mining is the practice of collecting data produced by an implantable device that monitors bodily processes for commercial interests.
details: As an android is a human-like robot, a cyborg, on the other hand, is an organism whose physiological functioning is aided by or dependent upon a mechanical/electronic device that relies on some sort of feedback. Implantable cybernetics and biomechatronics are on course to be proliferated among the global population within the twenty-first century as the markets for implantable electronics are already huge and growing. The global market for artificial cardiac pacemakers (PMs) and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) was approximately €8 billion in 2015, and is growing at 10% per year. Over 350 million people worldwide experience endemic diseases, diabetes, cardiac and renal failure, hearing disorders, and neurological disorders, thus making implantable technologies specific to these uses susceptible to increasingly higher demand. However, for the millions of cyborgs already equipped with body-enhancing technologies, namely PMs and ICDs, the data mining of these technologies pertains to broader topics of data sovereignty, data ownership rights, privacy and security, and medical research and development.

explainer.lead: Cyborg data mining means collecting data from an implanted device that monitors the body and using that data for commercial interests. It matters because people with devices such as pacemakers may not control who owns, accesses, or profits from information about their bodies.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a tiny device inside your body that keeps notes about how your heart is working. Cyborg data mining is when those notes are collected to serve business interests, not just to help you stay healthy. That raises questions about who owns the notes and who is allowed to read them.
tiers.practitioner: This arises where implantable-device monitoring meets data collection and commercial analysis. Engineers working around such systems need to address data ownership, access, privacy, security, and data sovereignty alongside medical and research uses. A key pitfall is treating technical access to bodily data as permission to exploit it commercially.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation, cyborg data mining concerns data D generated by an implantable device monitoring bodily processes, where D is collected or analysed for commercial interests. The concept sits within implantable cybernetics and biomechatronics and raises issues of data sovereignty, ownership rights, privacy, security, and medical research and development. Its scope is broader than any single implant or disease area.

explainer.example: A person with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator has cardiac processes monitored by the device. If data produced by that monitoring is collected and mined for commercial interests, the practice is cyborg data mining, and it raises the question of whether the patient controls that use.

usedIn.name: Artificial cardiac pacemakers
usedIn.detail: Pacemakers are body-enhancing implants whose monitoring data can raise questions about collection, ownership, and commercial use.

usedIn.name: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators
usedIn.detail: These cardiac implants are another established source of body-related data covered by the concept.

usedIn.name: Medical research and development
usedIn.detail: Data from body-enhancing implants connects commercial data mining with medical research, privacy, and security concerns.

explainer.intuition: An implant can turn ongoing bodily processes into valuable data. When that data is gathered for commercial interests, the person living with the device becomes part of a data system whose ownership and control may be disputed.
howItWorks: An implantable electronic device monitors one or more bodily processes.
The device produces data about those processes.
That data is collected from the implant-based system.
The collected data is mined or otherwise used to serve commercial interests.
Questions then arise about ownership, sovereignty, privacy, security, and permitted medical or research uses.
explainer.whyItMatters: Millions of people already use body-enhancing technologies such as pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, and demand for implantable electronics is growing. Commercial use of their bodily data makes ownership, consent, privacy, and security practical concerns rather than distant speculation.
misconceptions: It does not require a human-like robot: a cyborg here is an organism whose physiological functioning is aided by or dependent on a feedback-based mechanical or electronic device.
It is not limited to cardiac implants, although pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators are the clearest examples given.
It is not simply all medical use of implant data: the defining feature is collection for commercial interests.
